items.title: mount: keep hot directories cached
items.body:
Addresses the analysis in #10708: browsing a directory while another client keeps writing into it drives sustained CPU on the mount, because the cached listing keeps getting discarded and re-fetched.

The per-event handling was already incremental: the apply loop inserts or removes just the changed entry, versioned so late or duplicate events cannot roll the cache back. But the hot-directory heuristic sat on top of it, wiping the whole cached listing after 64 events within 2s and flipping the directory to read-through. With a continuous writer the directory cycles forever through wipe, full direct listing, full rebuild, and every sibling lookup in between falls through to the filer as its own LookupEntry call. The writer's own events also count toward the threshold, so a local untar evicts its own directory (the deferred-create fallback in lookupEntry papered over exactly that).

Since events keep a cached directory coherent, churn is no reason to discard it. This removes the churn wipe; idle eviction (-dirIdleEvictSec) and kernel Forget still bound memory, and directories over -cacheDirMaxEntries still read through as before. The second commit removes the directory-notification plumbing that existed only to drive the wipe.

items.title: heartbeat: keep the master current through collection churn
items.body:
Since #10640 the basic-s3 CI jobs fail nondeterministically: random tests hit InternalError on PutObject after retries, with the master logging hundreds of "No writable volumes" and eventually "no free volumes left" despite the volume server holding a dozen volumes. Reproduced locally with bucket create/put/delete churn against a CI-shaped all-in-one server; four interacting causes, one commit each.

Deleting a collection told the master nothing. The volume server left the master to work out what went by omission from the next full list -- store.go said so in a comment -- and delta mode took that list away. The volumes a bucket's churn creates and destroys between two full-list requests are never named in either direction, so the master goes on counting their slots: 100 slots occupied against 7 volumes on disk, until an unrelated repair happens to ask for the whole list. The destroy path already knows which volumes it removed, so it now sends them down the same channel every other deletion uses. Mirrored in the Rust volume server, whose notify path derives the same delta by diffing snapshots and was simply never woken.

Delta heartbeats said nothing about departed volumes. Deltas now name volumes gone since the last report, derived from the report state, which also matches what the Rust volume server already does. A volume that moved disks is not a departure. This covers deletions no channel announces -- an expired ttl -- rather than the collection case above.

Deleting a collection leaked its lookup-digest bits. Topology.DeleteCollection dropped the layouts wholesale without releasing per-node lookup ownership, so held and servable digests could never agree again and the master requested the full volume list on every heartbeat, forever, keeping the delta protocol from ever engaging.

A full list raced concurrent growth. A list collected before a grow finished cannot name the volumes the grow registered; applying it erased them, stranding the new collection without writable volumes. Volumes the master registered itself now survive reports that do not name them until a report confirms them (with a 10s cap so a registration that never materializes cannot linger); explicitly reported deletions still remove immediately.

The repro is 300 rounds of create bucket / put 6 objects / list / delete bucket against `weed server` with the CI's `-volume.max=100 -master.volumeSizeLimitMB=100`, counting master-side slot exhaustion:

| build | runtime | put failures | "no free volumes left" | full lists requested |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before #10640 | 109s | 0 | 105 | 0 |
| master | 234s | 3 | 342 | 23 |
| this PR | 89s | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Sampling the master's view of the node against the volume server's own count: before, the master pinned at 100 volumes for seconds at a time while the disk held 7; now it never sees more than the 7 that exist.

  - Ensured collection deletion reports removed volumes without affecting other collections.

items.title: windows mount: cache file data, resolved paths and attributes
items.body:
Fixes #10693.

The native Windows mount ran every operation bare, because the caches the kernel provides a unix mount do not exist on Windows unless the filesystem asks for them. WinFsp only turns the Windows cache manager on for a file when FileInfoTimeout is infinite, so at the old `attr_timeout=1` every application read and write was a synchronous trip into weed.exe at whatever size the application issued. And the adapter re-resolved the full path through Lookup on every operation, which in a directory the filer has not listed yet meant filer round trips per component, per operation — a stat cost ~3 of them.

The caching side:

- `FileInfoTimeout=-1` turns the cache manager on. Metadata events already reach FspFileSystemNotify, which purges a changed file's cached pages and attributes, so the infinite timeout stays coherent; the dir listing, volume info and EA timeouts are pinned to one second so they do not silently inherit the infinity.
- The adapter keeps a path cache that plays the part of the kernel's dentry and attribute caches: it owns one lookup reference per entry the way the kernel holds one until FORGET, serves attribute reads for files without an open handle, and is purged by the mount's own mutations and by metadata events, with a one-second timeout as backstop.
- Release moves the handle's reference back into the cache together with the file's final attributes — when the path still names that inode — so the stat that follows every copied file is served locally.

Running the mount tests against this exposed that Windows runs the FUSE flush after CloseHandle has already returned (only delete-carrying cleanups are waited), which broke three things that close(2)'s synchronous flush hides on Linux, one of them a latent bug on both platforms:

- Entry creation was deferred to the flush, so listings and renames raced unflushed closes: a directory listing missed just-written files, and renaming a directory moved it on the filer before its newest child existed there. The Windows mount now persists entries at create time.
- A truncate that shrinks a file trims its chunks, but written pages that had not become chunks yet were invisible to it, so the next flush wrote them back and the file grew again, resurrecting the truncated bytes. The shrink now flushes those pages into chunks first. This one is platform-neutral.
- Unlink set the handle's deleted flag without ordering against a flush already past its own check of that flag, so the flush could write the entry back right after the delete removed it, and a delete-on-close file outlived its last handle. The flag is now set and re-checked under the handle's flush lock.

Benchmarked on windows-latest against rclone mounting the same mini cluster's WebDAV endpoint through the same WinFsp, which is the comparison from the issue. The harness is `test/mount_bench`; the new workflow runs it on demand. Baseline phases reproduced within a few percent across runs.

| phase | before | after | rclone+WebDAV |
|---|---|---|---|
| seq_write | 665 MB/s | 669 MB/s | 1297 MB/s |
| seq_read | 93 MB/s | 2120 MB/s | 84 MB/s |
| rand_read 4k | 1849 ops/s | 130828 ops/s | 11639 ops/s |
| small_write 64k | 95 ops/s | 176 ops/s | 354 ops/s |
| small_read | 149 ops/s | 238 ops/s | 168 ops/s |
| stat_files | 259 ops/s | 1878 ops/s | 3001 ops/s |
| list_dir | 56 ops/s | 415 ops/s | 51 ops/s |
| overwrite | 84 ops/s | 1097 ops/s | 522 ops/s |
| delete | 129 ops/s | 333 ops/s | 839 ops/s |
| list 5k files | 71k entries/s | 163k entries/s | 42k entries/s |
| walk 5k files | 60k entries/s | 382k entries/s | 116k entries/s |

Writes and deletes still trail rclone because rclone acknowledges into its local vfs cache and uploads or deletes remotely later; the mount keeps close-means-persisted semantics on purpose.

items.title: mount: version open file handles by filer log position
items.body:
Fixes #10394

A metadata event refreshing an open handle re-looked the path up; a transient failure left the handle permanently pinned to its old entry, since the subscription cursor had already advanced. The first attempt to fix this (#10395) applied the event's entry directly, and review then found a sequence of rollback races: each fix manufactured an ordering signal out of band from the state it protected — a delivered-event cursor, a pre-RPC ping, a stable-read retry — and each approximation had a window the next reproduction lived in. This redoes the fix on a single invariant instead: the filer log position is the version of any filer state, and the version travels with the value.

Filer side, lookup and remote-cache responses now carry a log timestamp stamped before the serving read — events are logged after their store write on that clock, so everything at or below the stamp is provably reflected in the returned entry. Mutation acks already carry it in their returned event, and the mount's local store pairs each read with a version cursor advanced under the same lock as the store write.

Mount side, every handle records the version its entry reflects, and one rule replaces the per-site reasoning: state at or below the handle's version must not be installed. Invalidations apply the event's own entry with the event's version — no lookup, so no transient-failure window — except under a cached parent, where the store entry is the ordered merge of the event and anything applied since. Opens version fresh handles from the lookup response; flushes, truncates, and remote-cache downloads version from their acks. Directory builds version the completed directory at the listing snapshot and re-invalidate buffered events at that version.

The test suite replays every race found in the previous attempt as a deterministic reproduction against a fake filer: rollback of a newer local flush in queued, cached, and read-through configurations; stale leftovers under uncached parents; the build window including abort; handles opened after an event was queued; events landing mid-lookup; and undelivered events at remote-cache time across a filer failover.

Known residuals, inherent to per-filer clocks: multi-filer clock skew can make a fence conservatively skip one event until the next arrives, and eventless acks from pre-upgrade filers leave the handle unversioned, degrading to today's behavior. The server-side copy path installs its result unversioned and converges when the copy's own committed event is delivered.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Prevented open file handles and cached entries from being overwritten or rolled back by older metadata events by fencing refreshes with filer log/version timestamps (including save/update acknowledgements, renames/deletes, queued notifications, and remote-entry downloads).
  * Improved metadata cache version tracking so invalidations and buffered directory-build events are applied consistently.
  * Added filer response log-position timestamps to better support consistent acknowledgement handling.
* **Tests**
  * Expanded coverage for versioned invalidation, rollback fencing, buffering/directory build behavior, concurrent open races, and remote-cache failover scenarios.

items.title: topology: digest the volumes a master believes each node holds
items.body:
First step of the heartbeat change for #10603. Inert on its own — nothing reads the digest yet — but it is the piece the protocol rests on, so it seemed worth landing and reviewing separately.

## Why

A volume server resends its entire volume list every `VolumePulsePeriod`. That is not laziness: the full list is the only mechanism by which the master notices a volume that disappeared without a delta — a crash mid-delete, a pulled disk, a `DeletedVolumes` delta lost on a dropped stream. The self-heal block in `SyncDataNodeRegistration` exists because that divergence happens anyway.

So the list cannot simply be dropped; it has to be replaced by something that gives the same guarantee. A digest does: the two ends agree if and only if the master's copy is current. Steady state ships a digest and the handful of volumes that actually changed; a mismatch asks for the full list.

At the scale in #10603 that is 229MB and 28MB on the wire per heartbeat per volume server, every 5 seconds, becoming a few hundred bytes.

## What this does

`VolumeInfo.ReportHash` digests one volume. It has to cover **every** field of `VolumeInformationMessage` — a change the hash misses is a change the master would never be told about — so `TestVolumeDigestTracksEveryReportedField` mutates each of the sixteen fields in turn and asserts the hash moves.

Both ends run the same function over the same `storage.VolumeInfo`: the volume server over the message it is about to send, the master over what it already holds. There is no second implementation to drift. This is only possible now that #10610 and #10611 interned `ReplicaPlacement` and `TTL`, which made `NewVolumeInfo` allocation-free.

`Disk` keeps the xor of its volumes' hashes. Xor is order-independent, so the digest does not depend on report order, and it is its own inverse, so add/update/remove each stay O(1) by xoring a volume out before its old state is dropped and back in after the new one lands. No per-volume storage: the old `VolumeInfo` is already in the map.

`DataNode.VolumeDigest` xors across the node's disks.

## Cost

None measurable. `BenchmarkSyncDataNodeRegistration/100000Volumes` is unchanged at `23142019 B/op 200258 allocs/op`; the hash is allocation-free and the time difference is inside run-to-run noise.

## Next

1. `Heartbeat.volume_digest` + `HeartbeatResponse.resend_full_volume_list`, master compares and asks for a resend on mismatch. Volume servers keep sending full lists, so this only proves the two digests agree in production.
2. Volume server sends only changed volumes once the master has acked digest support, falling back to the full list on request.
3. Mirror into `seaweed-volume`.

Refs #10603

items.title: volume server: route VolumeMarkReadonly to raft leader
items.body:
## Problem

With HA masters (`-master.peers` / multiple `-master` on volume servers), `weed shell volume.mark`
fails after raft leader election:

```
error: set volume 7 readonly=true on master ctl-a:9333:
  raft.Server: Not current leader
```

while `cluster/status` on ctl-b reports `IsLeader: true`.

`weed shell` connects to the leader, but `volume.mark` goes through the volume server, which
calls `VolumeMarkReadonly` on `vs.GetMaster()` — the heartbeat peer, which may still be a
follower until the heartbeat stream redirects.

This breaks `volume.tier.move` (which marks replicas read-only before copying) and automation
that marks volumes read-only across elections.

## Fix

`notifyMasterVolumeReadonly` tries the heartbeat peer (`GetMaster`) first. If the master
returns `Not current leader`, resolve the raft leader via `GetMasterConfiguration` on
configured `-master` peers (followers already return `Leader`) and retry on that address.

`currentMaster` is **not** updated by leader lookup — the heartbeat loop owns that field and
reconnects when the stream reports a different leader than the connected peer.

Adds `operation.LookupRaftLeaderMaster` with unit tests.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test ./weed/operation -run LookupRaftLeader`
- [x] `go test ./weed/server -run LookupRaftLeaderMasterDoesNotUpdate`
- [x] `go test ./weed/operation ./weed/server` (CI build tags)

items.title: filer: add ObjectTransaction for atomic multi-entry object writes
items.body:
Replaces #9641 (GitHub auto-closed it after a force-push briefly left the branch with a zero-commit diff; it can't be reopened due to a stale head OID).

ObjectTransaction applies an ordered list of mutations (PUT / DELETE / PATCH_EXTENDED) atomically under one per-path lock (lock_key), with an optional WriteCondition checked first. Lets a caller describe a multi-entry object operation as one request instead of holding a distributed lock across several RPCs. DELETE/PATCH of an absent entry are no-ops (idempotent on replay).

items.title: fix(mount): avoid self-notify deadlock in Link and CopyFileRange handlers
items.body:
## Summary

- The `Link` handler's `syncHardLinkSiblings` (`weed/mount/weedfs_link.go:235`) and the `CopyFileRange` server-side-copy path's `invalidateCopyDestinationCache` (`weed/mount/weedfs_file_copy_range.go:504`) called `fuseServer.InodeNotify` / `EntryNotify` synchronously from inside a FUSE request handler. Notifications and replies share the same `/dev/fuse` fd, so the `syscall.Write` can block indefinitely when the kernel has not yet drained its queue — the mount then deadlocks.
- A goroutine dump from a stuck mount captured the `Link` handler blocked in `syscall.Write` inside `InodeNotify`, with every other goroutine idle (worker pools, gRPC keepalives, FUSE read loop waiting on the same fd).
- This patch drops those two synchronous notify calls. The local meta cache is still updated inline so subsequent filesystem ops see fresh state; the kernel's attr/dentry caches refresh once their TTL expires.

Note: this trades the eager kernel-cache invalidation for correctness. If the pjdfstest `link/00.t` regression that motivated the original `InodeNotify` re-appears because the kernel serves a stale `nlink` until attr TTL, we can re-introduce the notify asynchronously (`go wfs.fuseServer.InodeNotify(...)`) in a follow-up instead of reverting this fix.

items.title: [s3] Cleaning uploads can cause corruption [LOW RISK]
items.body:
When running `s3.clean.uploads` which is enabled by default in the admin script worker (weed scaffold -config=master), it cleans files under `.uploads` and deletes their contents as well. A successful upload takes those chunks and then does a metadata delete on those files so that there is only one referent per file chunk. If an error occurred when metadata-deleting the `.uploads` files, the admin script would delete the chunks from the completed file as the partial files reference them. The error is simply logged only at V(1+) and ignored. This is low risk because the metadata file deletion would have to fail or the s3 server would have to go offline right before it deletes the directory. 

The easiest way to fix this is to look at the `SeaweedFSUploadId` while pruning files in `.uploads` to determine if the multipart chunks assembled into a complete file. If such a file exists, simply do a metadata delete instead.

The other one is to use the filer's `ObjectTransaction` request to apply the following under a lock when completing an upload
1. Put the new version in with all the chunks
2. Delete old metadata
3. Update the latest version

Everything runs in order, no roll back, exits on the first failure, and things are committed in order, and observable partial states are completely safe. If step 2 fails, the upload is failed and the stray version is cleaned up. If the stray version fails to be cleaned up then it can also cause complications but that is pre-existing and out of scope for this issue.

Example patch 
<details>

```diff
diff --git a/weed/s3api/s3api_multipart_finalize_txn.go b/weed/s3api/s3api_multipart_finalize_txn.go
new file mode 100644
--- /dev/null
+++ b/weed/s3api/s3api_multipart_finalize_txn.go
@@ -0,0 +1,139 @@
+package s3api
+
+import (
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/weed/glog"
+	"github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/weed/pb"
+	"github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/weed/pb/filer_pb"
+	"github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/weed/s3api/s3err"
+)
+
+// routedMultipartFinalize commits a completed multipart upload in ONE
+// ObjectTransaction on the owner filer, instead of three separate RPCs:
+//
+//  1. PUT     <object>.versions/<versionFile> (the finished object)
+//  2. DELETE  <bucket>/.uploads/<uploadId>   (metadata only)
+//  3. RECOMPUTE_LATEST on <object>.versions   (publish it as current)
+//
+// Why this exists rather than extending routedVersionedFinalize: that helper is
+// shared with CopyObject and createDeleteMarker, neither of which has an upload
+// directory or writes its entry inside the transaction. Keeping the multipart
+// shape here leaves those call sites untouched.
+//
+// Why the upload directory is removed with IsDeleteData=false: a multipart
+// object's chunks ARE the part chunks. Completion references the fids, it does
+// not copy bytes, so freeing them would destroy the object being published.
+// After this transaction the upload directory no longer exists, so
+// s3.clean.uploads has nothing to mistake for an abandoned upload.
+//
+// ORDER MATTERS, and not for the usual reason. ObjectTransaction holds one
+// per-path lock for the whole request (filer_grpc_server.go:305-307), which
+// gives isolation from other writers of the same object — but the mutation loop
+// applies each mutation in turn and returns on the first error with NO rollback
+// and no store-level transaction (filer_grpc_server.go:333-339). So a partial
+// application is reachable, and the order decides which partial states exist:
+//
+//	PUT, DELETE, RECOMPUTE   (this order)
+//	  fail at 1 -> nothing happened; the client can retry the completion
+//	  fail at 2 -> version file written but not current, upload directory still
+//	               there: BOTH reference the chunks, so nothing is unreferenced.
+//	               The caller rolls the version file back and the state is exactly
+//	               stock's "upload not completed" -- fully retryable.
+//	  fail at 3 -> version exists but is not current; the read-path heal and the
+//	               background reconciler both promote it
+//
+// Two orderings are wrong, for opposite reasons:
```

- A multipart object's chunks are the part chunks — completion references the fids, it doesn't copy bytes. Say this first; everything else follows from it.

items.title: Use filer-side copy for mounted whole-file copy_file_range
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

Mounted `cp` was still copying whole files through the mount process even when the kernel issued a full-file `copy_file_range()` request. That kept copies inside a mounted SeaweedFS bucket much slower than they need to be.

# How are we solving the problem?

- Detect the narrow whole-file `copy_file_range()` case in the mount layer and delegate it to the filer `cp.from` path instead of buffering the full file through dirty pages.
- Reuse the configured filer HTTP client path so the fast path honors HTTPS settings, uses a bounded request timeout, and attaches filer JWT auth when configured.
- Invalidate destination inode/entry cache after the server-side copy so the kernel sees the new size and metadata immediately.
- Allow the filer copy endpoint to overwrite the pre-created empty destination file that FUSE `cp` opens before `copy_file_range()` runs.
- Refresh destination timestamps on filer-side copies so the copied file gets new `mtime`/`crtime`.

Run the benchmark correctly

items.body:
Chris:
Today I found one volume file become read only(id: 3002) after compaction, so I took time to find out the root cause

Below is my online log:
```
I0206 06:56:50 17728 volume_server_handlers_vacuum.go:16] checked compacting volume = 2957 garbageThreshold = 0.1 vacuum = false
I0206 06:56:50 17728 volume_server_handlers_vacuum.go:16] checked compacting volume = 3002 garbageThreshold = 0.1 vacuum = true
I0206 06:56:51 17728 volume_server_handlers_vacuum.go:25] compacted volume = 3002 , error = <nil>
I0206 06:56:51 17728 volume_loading.go:62] open to write file /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.idx
I0206 06:56:51 17728 volume_loading.go:69] volumeDataIntegrityChecking failed verifyNeedleIntegrity /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_
3002.idx failed: File Entry Not Found. Needle 5040252 Memory 5040257
I0206 06:56:51 17728 volume_loading.go:73] loading index file /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.idx readonly true
I0206 06:56:51 17728 needle_map_memory.go:51] max file key: 258388066 for file: /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.idx
I0206 06:56:51 17728 volume_server_handlers_vacuum.go:34] commit compact volume = 3002 , error = <nil>
```
From above volume log,  we could conclude that the volumeDataIntegrityChecking failed after the 3002 volume is compacted.

But when I restart this volume server, everything seems to be OK
```
Log file created at: 2017/02/06 11:30:38
Running on machine: xxxxxxxxx
Binary: Built with gc go1.7.3 for linux/amd64
Log line format: [IWEF]mmdd hh:mm:ss threadid file:line] msg
I0206 11:30:38 51565 file_util.go:20] Folder /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume Permission: -rwxrwxr-x
I0206 11:30:38 51565 volume_loading.go:62] open to write file /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.idx
I0206 11:30:38 51565 volume_loading.go:73] loading index file /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.idx readonly false
I0206 11:30:38 51565 needle_map_memory.go:51] max file key: 258388066 for file: /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.idx
I0206 11:30:38 51565 disk_location.go:64] data file /data/seaweedfs/weed-volume/lawsuit-bucket_3002.dat, replicaPlacement=101 v=2 size=39271144 ttl=
```

And I suspect that the Needle's ReadData function get the cached needle data by mistake which lead to the following error:
3002.idx failed: File Entry Not Found. Needle 5040252 Memory 5040257

Because the current block cache key format is:
`cacheKey := fmt.Sprintf("%d:%d:%d", r.Fd(), offset>>3, readSize)`
If the fid is reused by OS and one needle's offset in old dat file and new compacted dat file is same(their file size diff is less than the needle alignment padding size), then the cache hitting is triggered. This is actually a edge case, but it did happen

Do you have any suggestion on this scenario? 
Thanks!
